source.verification_method: All 22 supplied pages, footnotes, eight-part classification, all discrete/unified examples and complete bibliography read. Page 13 classification visually inspected. citation.title: The Architecture of Moral Responsibility: Re-Structuring Moral Blame to fill in the Responsibility gap

reading.source_scope_note: A philosophical reconstruction of responsibility distinguishes evaluative attributability, accountability, answerability and culpability, then proposes eight combinations illustrated with fictional cases. Under the author’s framework, AI contributes causally/functionally but does not bear moral responsibility; humans and institutions remain accountable. No participants, model experiment, legal finding or empirical validation of the taxonomy is supplied.
access_limits: Complete supplied text, all footnotes and bibliography read. No substantive figures or numbered data tables are present. Page 13 eight-part list was visually checked. Publisher Data Availability correctly identifies theoretical/conceptual analysis; no Supplementary section was located.

Watson 2019 Second Thoughts DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198830238.003.0011 and other selected references were metadata-verified only. Watson’s full original chapter, Wolf’s book and the quoted philosophical originals were not separately fully read here. Do not present the supplied author’s reconstruction as an independently verified exact reading of each original.

JSTOR metadata at https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv24w64ch identifies Paul Dumouchel and Luisa Damiano as authors and Malcolm DeBevoise as translator. The book itself was not fully read; access to the full book was not available in that inspected session. No access restriction was bypassed.

The Senate-hosted PDF linked by footnote 5 exceeded the web tool’s content-size limit, about 15 MB, and was not read. Its filename indicates testimony, but it may contain attachments; no claim is made that the cited court order is necessarily absent. No docket, current case outcome or complete court record was reviewed.

Real chatbot incidents are secondary allegations and news examples in this philosophical paper. They are not adjudicated causation, a new clinical study or prevalence evidence. No identifiable user narratives, self-harm details or allegations are turned into new behavioral source counts.

No raw data, author-code execution, private access, author contact, full-paper Markdown archive or independent replication. Military vignettes are conceptual responsibility examples, not operational instructions or legal advice.

study.type: Normative and conceptual philosophical argument. The author explicitly reports no empirical data or studies with human participants. Historical/fictional illustrations and reported lawsuits do not convert the paper into an observed AI-behavior study.
study.core_distinction: Watsonian attributability concerns what conduct expresses about an agent’s evaluative orientation. Accountability concerns standing interpersonal demands, justification and possible sanction. Answerability has capacity, reason-responsive and interpersonal-obligation senses. Culpability concerns warranted blame under relevant conditions. These relations can come apart; causation alone does not determine any of them.
study.ai_position: The author excludes present AI from moral agency, subjecthood and all four Watsonian relations. System-level attributive assessment instead maps causal/functional machine contributions to human and institutional decisions. This is the paper’s defended philosophical position, not an experimentally established universal incapacity or a settled answer across the corpus.
study.human_ownership: The framework emphasizes non-delegable human/institutional accountability and aims to trace design, deployment, oversight, knowledge and role obligations. Recognizing technical contributions does not itself transfer moral fault to software or erase relevant human duties.
study.eight_dimensions: Page 13 constructs eight combinations of attribution/accountability/culpability. Several overlap by design; the paper supplies no mutually exclusive coding rule, unique coverage proof, independent factors, reliability test or validated scoring instrument. Preserve their definitions and examples in review metadata rather than mint eight independent behavior rows.
study.examples: Wolf-inspired Jojo cases and hypothetical drone chains illustrate role, endorsement, knowledge, coercion and control. Later a single integrated scenario repeats all eight perspectives. These are analytic stipulations, not observed incidents, legal determinations or proof the framework improves investigation accuracy.
study.nonculpable_scope: Non-culpable accountability is first described with mitigated culpability under epistemic/coercive constraints; later examples stipulate reasonable epistemic limits. Mitigated blame and absence of blame are not identical. Keep the source’s label while recording that unresolved boundary rather than treating all misinformation or coercion as complete exculpation.
study.synthetic_ethics: Earlier passages expressly restrict synthetic ethics to descriptive co-evolutionary context and decline to adopt the original method; the conclusion calls the developed account a framework of synthetic ethics. This terminology needs care, not an invented consensus or a new ethical principle for the project.
study.agency_language: Section Agency Without Responsibility and occasional references to attributability of AI are qualified by the explicit distinction between Watsonian moral attributability and system-level attribution. Do not report that the paper grants AI moral blame merely because it uses attribution language.
study.institutional_limits: The claim that institutional actors can bear duties differs from asserting literal individual consciousness or identical moral capacities. Institutions’ responsibility, individual agency and an AI component’s causal role should not be conflated. The philosophical framework does not establish a universal current-law liability rule.
study.cases: Lawsuits and news about conversational systems motivate concern but are not controlled evidence or final findings. Broad statements that a chatbot caused vulnerability exceed what the philosophical reconstruction independently establishes. Current proceedings and clinical effects are not adjudicated here.
study.scope: No proof that every responsibility gap is closed, every prior theory lacks guidance, eight relations are exhaustive or distinct, human accountability is enforceable in practice, or no future AI can satisfy any theory of responsibility. A refined vocabulary is different from a demonstrated institutional remedy.

analytical_dimensions.name: Attributive accountability
analytical_dimensions.definition: Conduct expresses an agent’s evaluative commitments and places the agent under interpersonal accountability.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Overlapping conceptual combination; no new independent row.

analytical_dimensions.name: Non-attributive accountability
analytical_dimensions.definition: Accountability attaches through a role or institution even when conduct does not express personal evaluative commitments.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Existing role responsibility covers the principal distinction.

analytical_dimensions.name: Accountable attribution
analytical_dimensions.definition: Attributable conduct generates standing interpersonal demands for explanation, apology or justification.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Keep its source label; overlap with attributive accountability is not empirically resolved.

analytical_dimensions.name: Non-accountable attribution
analytical_dimensions.definition: Conduct or traits can be evaluatively attributed without a resulting interpersonal demand for justification.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: A qualification of attributability rather than a newly identified independent behavior.

analytical_dimensions.name: Culpable accountability
analytical_dimensions.definition: The accountable agent meets conditions for warranted blame.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Normative combination, not an independent measured psychological mechanism.

analytical_dimensions.name: Non-culpable accountability
analytical_dimensions.definition: Accountability persists while epistemic or coercive constraints mitigate or remove culpability.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Retain source ambiguity between mitigation and complete absence of blame; not an exact synonym of reparative blameless responsibility.

analytical_dimensions.name: Culpable attributability
analytical_dimensions.definition: Conduct expresses a defective evaluative orientation that warrants character-based blame.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: Normative intersection, not new independent behavior evidence.

analytical_dimensions.name: Non-culpable attributability
analytical_dimensions.definition: Conduct reflects features of the agent without warranting blame.
analytical_dimensions.catalogue_decision: An existing concept’s boundary; attribution and blame must remain separate.

summary: No new record. Retain all eight proposed combinations as explicit review metadata mapped to existing concepts. Enrich attributability, answerability, role responsibility, blame, many-hands analysis and the retribution gap. Distinguish human/institutional duties from system-level causal assessment and retain philosophical disagreement with earlier corpus sources. Correct verified chapter metadata, author segmentation and translator credit without claiming full original-source reading.

findings.definition: A sense of moral responsibility concerned with whether an agent’s conduct warrants a moral assessment of the agent’s qualities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The author distinguishes moral evaluability expressing an agent’s commitments from system-level causal/functional attribution. AI is excluded from the former within this framework but remains part of the latter analysis.
findings.boundary: This is a normative position, not a model test. Earlier read sources defend different conditions for possible AI attributability; do not erase that disagreement, change the concept into mere causation or infer settled actual machine mental capacities.

findings.definition: Being expected and able to give reasons for one’s actions or decisions to the people affected by them.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: A secondary reconstruction distinguishes the capacity to respond, rational engagement with criticism and a standing obligation to justify conduct to others. Generated answers are distinguished from occupying a normative interpersonal role.
findings.boundary: The source’s only-human conclusion is philosophical, not empirically proven. Fluent explanations and causal responsiveness do not establish faithful justification or discharge the institution’s duties. Full original Watson text was not independently read here.

findings.definition: Having duties and being evaluated for their fulfillment because of a specific role.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: Accountability can attach to institutional role occupancy without personal endorsement of a policy; later examples separate operators, developers and command/oversight structures.
findings.boundary: Role, legitimate duty, actual control, knowledge and culpability remain separate. A role label or obedience does not by itself prove either deserved punishment or complete exculpation. Do not move institutional accountability onto an unsupported operator or machine.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The eight proposed combinations separate evaluative attribution, interpersonal demands and warranted blame under epistemic/coercive conditions. Not every attributable outcome or role duty warrants censure.
findings.boundary: The combinations are conceptual and overlapping, not eight measured behaviors or a validated blame scale. No actual incident fault, legal liability or universal allocation rule is demonstrated.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper traces distributed design, procurement, command, operation and governance contributions in hypothetical sociotechnical chains and argues against assuming that distributed contributions erase accountability.
findings.boundary: These are conceptual illustrations, not observed prevalence or proof of enforceable closure. Many contributors do not imply nobody is accountable, and technical involvement is not identical to moral agency.

findings.definition: A mismatch between a desire for retributive punishment and the absence of an appropriate target for it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: Background reports Danaher’s mismatch between retributive expectations and absence of a suitable punishment target, distinct from other responsibility relations.
findings.boundary: A secondary conceptual citation, not new evidence of public punishment demands or proof that no responsible human/institution exists. Retribution, warranted blame, investigation and remedy must remain separate.

findings.definition: Taking an appropriate role in acknowledging and redressing harm connected to one’s agency despite the absence of blameworthiness for causing it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The author proposes accountability despite mitigated culpability, with later role examples under reasonable knowledge limits.
findings.boundary: Context only:mitigation is not absence of blame, and role accountability is not the earlier source’s specific relational duty to acknowledge/redress faultless harm. Preserve the related distinctions without merging exact names or claiming measured repair effects.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity the capacity to understand moral considerations, make ethical judgments and bear responsibility for its choices.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The framework refuses to treat AI as a moral agent and assigns technical components a causal/functional analytical role.
findings.boundary: Context only:this is not a participant attribution study or empirical test of actual agency, consciousness or normative capacity. Moral agency and legal personality differ; the author’s theory does not resolve every alternative philosophical account.

findings.definition: Diluting felt personal responsibility for harmful conduct by treating responsibility as shared among multiple actors.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The paper rejects treating distribution across humans/institutions and technical components as automatic dilution of accountability.
findings.boundary: Context only:no reduced felt responsibility, disengagement, behavior or diffusion manipulation is measured. A sociotechnical allocation difficulty is not evidence of a psychological diffusion effect.

findings.definition: Reduced human decision ownership when an AI tool significantly influences a decision through value judgments the decision-maker has not endorsed.
findings.novelty_rationale: Retain existing responsibility concepts. The source proposes combinations of normative relations, not eight empirically independent psychological mechanisms; conceptual disagreements must remain attributed to their authors.
findings.evidence_scope: The conclusion describes several misalignments among responsibility relations under technological mediation.
findings.boundary: Context only:this broad proposed taxonomy is not a new test of the narrower existing unendorsed-value/decision-ownership gap. Do not treat all responsibility gaps as exact synonyms or infer ownership loss in actual users.

source_corrections.finding: The DOI identifies Matthias Scheutz, The Need for Moral Competency in Autonomous Agent Architectures, a 2016 chapter in Fundamental Issues of Artificial Intelligence, pages 517–527, online 8 June 2016. The supplied 2014 / Moral Competence in Autonomous Systems container is not the verified DOI record. Content was not fully read here.

Correct first author is Filippo Santoni de Sio, with Giulio Mecacci; de Santoni, F. incorrectly truncates/resegments the name. Verified article is Philosophy & Technology 34(4):1057–1084, online 14 May 2021. No independent full reading credit is added here.

Paul Dumouchel and Luisa Damiano are the authors; Malcolm DeBevoise is credited as translator. Preserve translator credit separately rather than list a third coauthor. Book content was not fully read.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: The supplied Do people punish robots? Blame, punishment, and forgiveness in human–robot interaction, Frontiers in Psychology 12:659154, was not independently verified. The constructed candidate DOI 10.3389/fpsyg.2021.659154 returned Crossref 404 and targeted title search did not establish a correct record. Do not label it fabricated, silently substitute another robot study or count it as verified empirical support.

Namvarpour/Pauwels/Razi 2025 is cited in a footnote without a full bibliography entry. The claimed corpus and counts were not independently verified or converted into source credit. Store as an unresolved pointer, not confirmed harassment prevalence or observed clinical causation.

Attributive accountability and accountable attribution both connect evaluative attribution with interpersonal demands. The paper offers no operational boundary proving disjointness or independent mechanisms. Retain both source labels in review metadata without eight new catalogue rows.

Initial definition uses mitigated culpability, whereas the name and later examples can imply absence of fault. Mitigation, exculpation, role responsibility and reparative duty should not be silently equated.

Full Watson/Wolf originals and quoted claims about corporations, impaired agency and synthetic ethics were not independently checked in complete originals. Preserve as the supplied author’s reconstruction and note philosophical disagreement, rather than declare universal premises empirically established.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: Real chatbot lawsuits and testimony link
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Allegations, company defenses and a secondary testimony pointer are not final causal/legal findings. The linked large PDF was not read; its filename alone does not prove that a court order is missing from attachments. Current case outcomes were not established.

The vocabulary is not accompanied by an implementation, assignment algorithm, institutional trial or comparative evidence that prior theories lack guidance. Mapping responsibility can aid analysis, but practical closure of gaps and efficacy remain untested.

refuted_suspected_errors.finding: The author repeatedly distinguishes Watsonian moral relations from system-level causal/functional assessment and retains human/institutional accountability. Attribution language alone does not justify the stronger reading.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Theoretical Data Availability contradicts an experiment
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: Unlike the previous PDF, this paper consistently identifies conceptual analysis and reports no new empirical dataset. Thought experiments are not missing participant data.

refuted_suspected_errors.location: Eight labels establish eight independent behaviors
refuted_suspected_errors.finding: They are proposed combinations of responsibility relations with stipulated examples. Neither independent psychological mechanisms nor empirical factor distinctness is demonstrated.
Legitimate shared duties and technical contributions can coexist with clear human accountability. No diminished felt responsibility was measured.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Earlier How AI Systems Can Be Blameworthy defends possible attributability under a different philosophical account. Preserve this substantive disagreement: neither conceptual paper empirically settles actual machine moral capacities.
Absence of blame can coexist with obligations after harm, but non-culpable role accountability and relational redress are not exact synonyms. Keep fault, authorship and remedy separate.
Role evaluation and human-like moral accountability differ. A technical component can be scrutinized without assigning it legal liability or erasing institutional duties.
Many-hands allocation, retributive dissatisfaction and psychological diffusion are distinct. Conceptual taxonomy is not a new causal study.
Do not confuse perceived moral approval, normative justification and actual institutional performance. A conceptual distinction or public preference does not determine moral truth.

deferred.term: Eight responsibility combinations as eight new behaviors
deferred.reason: Preserved completely under analytical_dimensions, mapped to existing concepts. They are overlapping normative intersections rather than demonstrated independent mechanisms.

deferred.term: System-level attributive assessment as a new behavior row
deferred.reason: Useful incident-analysis method mapping causal/functional contributions to responsible humans/institutions. Existing blame attribution, role responsibility and many-hands concepts cover the operational distinction; retain methodology rather than inflate behavior count.

deferred.term: Shotgun pleading as an AI behavior
deferred.reason: A legal pleading category mentioned as context, not a new model behavior or a verified finding about present litigation.

deferred.term: Culpable inadvertence as a new established mechanism
deferred.reason: Only briefly named in the reconstruction; no sufficiently developed independent definition or original-source reading here. Negligence, knowledge limits and warranted blame require distinct assessment.

deferred.term: Synthetic ethics as a new project principle
deferred.reason: The source uses a restricted contextual meaning and proposes a philosophical framework. It does not authorize replacement or expansion of the project’s six ethical principles.

limitations: Zero new catalogue records; six existing concepts receive bounded conceptual evidence and four receive non-counted context. All eight source subdivisions are preserved in structured review metadata. Catalogue remains 782 records in eleven categories, with stable IDs, unnumbered rows, seven evaluation criteria and six ethical principles. No automatic harm links, invented annual totals, forced citation quota, full-paper Markdown archive or empirical/clinical/legal validation claim.
